McWilliams Letter To Lockyer Blasts Lungren;
Nominates Kubby To Vaconcellos Committee

See
Peter McWilliams Sues Lungren For Failing to Enforce Prop 215; Seeks His Impeachment
and
California AG Lockyer Convenes Medical Marijuana
Task Force Led By State Senator Vasconcellos

From Peter McWilliams
8165 Mannix Drive
Los Angeles, California 90046

To The Honorable William Lockyer
Office of the Attorney General
1300 I Street
Suite 1740
Sacramento, California 95814
916-324-5437

March 18, 1999

Dear Attorney General Lockyer:

I am an AIDS patient and recent cancer survivor. I am the author of,"AIN’T NOBODY’S BUSINESS IF YOU DO. (http://www.mcwilliams.com/books/aint/index) I own a Los Angeles-based publishing company, Prelude Press, Inc.

I understand from an article in the San Jose Mercury News that you will be meeting next month with federal authorities on ways to implement Proposition 215.

All I can say is, thank you. It’s good to have an Attorney General in California again.

I have been a friend of John Vasconcellos for decades. He released a statement about my case

"http://206.41.12.194/mcwilliams/motion1/temp/senjohn/senjohn.htm"

and wrote an eloquent op-ed piece published in the February 25, 1999, Los Angeles Times. "http://www.petertrial.com/latimes.htm"

But it is not just classic liberals such as John who have written about my case. Classic conservatives have been appalled by the federal government encroachment on California law as represented in my case. William F. Buckley, Jr. has written about it in his syndicated column three times now.

"http://www.marijuanamagazine.com/toc/buckley.htm"

"http://www.marijuanamagazine.com/toc/082498-5.htm"

"http://www.petertrial.com/buckley.htm"

The Los Angeles Times February 26, 1999, article on my situation is at

"http://www.petertrial.com/lat.htm" http://www.petertrial.com/lat.htm

Since my dual diagnosis in March 1996, I have used medical marijuana under the guidance and supervision of three California physicians to fight the nausea caused by the prescription anti-AIDS and anti-cancer medications I must take.

If I cannot keep down my life-saving medications, I will die. Medical marijuana, in my case, had been 99.9 percent effective in alleviating nausea for more than two years.

On July 23, 1998, I was arrested by DEA Special Agents and charged with nine counts of marijuana cultivation, possession, intent to distribute, and a variety of conspiracy charges related to marijuana. No other drugs are mentioned in the indictment, nor are there any overt acts of sale or even purchase; no cash or firearms were found.

Two of my co-conspirators are fellow medical marijuana patients. Each has a California doctor’s written recommendation for medical marijuana. Each is a California resident. The remaining co-conspirators merely happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

I will not take the time to delineate my defense here. I can state that what I was doing was fully covered by California Health and Safety Code Section 11362.5, the 1996 California Compassionate Use Act, also known as Proposition 215.

Because I cannot keep down my prescription medications without medical marijuana forbidden me by my bail release my viral load has risen dramatically, from undetectable (under 40) to more than 250,000. AIDS doctors become concerned when the viral load tops 10,000. When I had non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma in 1996, the second most common AIDS-related cancer, my viral load never went above 12,500.

(Please see the letter from my AIDS physician, Daniel Bowers, M.D. at "http://www.petertrial.com/doc1.jpg"

Also of interest is the letter in support of my medical marijuana use from the doctor widely quoted by anti-medical-marijuana groups as saying, If your doctor recommends marijuana as treatment, you’ve got a lousy doctor. "http://www.petertrial.com/doc2a.jpg", "http://www.petertrial.com/doc2b.jpg"

I have an emergency motion before the Hon. George King in Los Angeles district federal court. The arguments were heard on February 26, 1999. It asked him to lift my bail restrictions on using medical marijuana, or, in the alternative, to order that I be enrolled as the ninth patient receiving medical marijuana from the federal government. (Complete briefings are at "http://www.petertrial.com" www.petertrial.com.) I await his written ruling.

I thought you might be able to use some of the research I did for a lawsuit filed against your predecessor, Mr. Lungren, about the duty of the California Attorney General when it comes to federal law vs. California law, as laid out by the California Constitution.

1. The California Constitution, Article III Section 3.5 states: An administrative agency [which includes the Office of the Attorney General] has no power . . . to declare a statute unenforceable or to refuse to enforce a statute on the basis that federal law or federal regulations prohibit the enforcement of such statute unless an appellate court has made a determination.

The simple brush-off made by your predecessor, Mr. Lungren, about 11362.5, Federal law supercedes state law is not always the case. In fact, according to my reading of the California Constitution and the input of several attorneys I have consulted, the Attorney General of California must fight such federal encroachment on California law until an appellate court has made a determination.

As you know, no appellate court has made a determination as to the federal government’s power to interfere with the private medical treatment given by licensed California physicians and the laws of California protecting the sick. In fact, 11362.5 has never even been challenged in court, unlike many other initiatives passed by California voters.

2. The California Constitution, Article III Section 3 states: Persons charged with the exercise of one power (legislative, executive or judicial) may not exercise either of the others except as permitted by this Constitution.

Your predecessor, Mr. Lungren, exercised the power of the judiciary, giving his own extremely narrow and limited interpretation of 11362.5 the full force and effect of law. Frankly, if the federal government cannot be won over by persuasion to permit Californians to enjoy the benefits of 11362.5, then it is a matter for the courts to decide. The California Constitution, in two places, encourages you, if necessary, to file suit against the federal government, asking that at least an appellate court make a determination before the federal government can move against citizens of California.

3. The California Constitution, Article V Section 13 states: The Attorney General has the duty to see that the laws of the state are . . . adequately enforced. The American Heritage Dictionary defines adequate as Sufficient to satisfy a requirement or meet a need. and enforced as, To compel observance of or obedience to,

Let’s review how adequately the Compassionate Use Act of 1996 has been enforced by your predecessor. Allow me to quote the three major elements of 11362.5 and compare each with my own present situation:

(A) To ensure that seriously ill Californians have the right to obtain and use marijuana for medical purposes where that medical use is deemed appropriate and has been recommended by a physician who has determined that the person’s health would benefit from the use of marijuana in the treatment of cancer, anorexia, AIDS, chronic pain, spasticity, glaucoma, arthritis, migraine, or any other illness for which marijuana provides relief.

Your predecessor certainly did nothing to ensure me of the right to obtain and use marijuana for medical purposes. Indeed, if I use medical marijuana today, the federal authorities will take away my disabled mother’s house and my brother’s house and put me in jail until the trial, currently scheduled for September such are the terms of my $250,000 release bond. (I spent a month in federal custody.)

(B) To ensure that patients and their primary caregivers who obtain and use marijuana for medical purposes upon the recommendation of a physician are not subject to criminal prosecution or sanction.

(I spent a month in federal custody.)

(B) To ensure that patients and their primary caregivers who obtain and use marijuana for medical purposes upon the recommendation of a physician are not subject to criminal prosecution or sanction.

Again, the Attorney General office has yet to do anything to ensure this provision. Consequently, I am facing a mandatory ten-year (possible life) sentence and a $4,000,000 fine all for actions covered under 11362.5.

(C) To encourage the federal and state governments to implement a plan to provide for the safe and affordable distribution of marijuana to all patients in medical need of marijuana.

(C) To encourage the federal and state governments to implement a plan to provide for the safe and affordable distribution of marijuana to all patients in medical need of marijuana.

Here your predecessor not only failed, but waged his own campaign against this very clear mandate from the people of California. When you fulfill this portion of California Law, I will not be in any further jeopardy.

Allow me to give but two recent examples of Western-state Attorneys General who have acted courageously and, in one case, against her personal convictions to fulfill their Oaths of Office and the laws of their states against federal encroachment. You will hardly be alone in taking on the federal government on behalf of the laws of your state.

First, consider Oregon’s physician-assisted suicide law. The federal government was, and is, uniformly against this referendum and firmly in favor of the federal government, through the DEA, stepping in. Here is an excerpt from an April 1998 letter sent to Attorney General Reno from 138 members of Congress, including then-House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senator Orrin Hatch, and Rep. Henry Hyde, the latter two, as you know, chair the Senate and House Judiciary Committees:

A decision by a state to rescind its own penalties for assisting a suicide cannot supersede federal laws, compel federal support or remove federal responsibility to uniformly enforce laws passed by Congress and approved by the president.

Sound familiar? The same tirade the same people are making against medical marijuana and California’s Compassionate Use Act. Among the signers of the letter were 34 senators, including seven members of the 18-member Senate Judiciary Committee. Of 104 signers in the House, 12 are members of the 35-member House Judiciary Committee. Those committees oversee the Justice Department. Only six members of Congressóall five Oregon Democrats plus Rep. Barney Frank of Massachusettsóhave argued that the federal government should not intervene in Oregon law.

Nevertheless, Oregon’s Attorney General, Hardy Myers, stood firm, maintaining that the central issue is the question of who has the authority to control the practice of medicine the federal government or the states. Oregon voters have made the decision that assisted suicide is a legitimate medical purpose.

Attorney General Myers continued: Our view is that this agency [the DEA] does not have the authority to interpret medical purpose in a way that interferes with Oregon’s assisted-suicide law.

Here an Attorney General fought the federal government for the right of a state to have physicians kill people. Surely, you could just as successfully argue that physicians can recommend a medicine that has never caused an overdose or allergic-reaction death in 5,000 known years of medicinal use.

The result? Although DEA Administrator Thomas Constantine made a public statement that the DEA would move in an override the Oregon law, Attorney General Reno (in what must have been the first time a U.S. Attorney General has not given the DEA whatever it wanted) contradicted the Administrator, and declared that the DEA would not move against that law of Oregon.

And, might I point out that you have a slightly more formidable appearance than Attorney General Myer?

A second example is Colorado’s Attorney General, Gale Norton’s, vigorous defense of the state referendum measure, Amendment 2. She took it all the way to U.S. Supreme Court.

Amendment 2 limited gay rights. Attorney General Norton’s personal belief and political stance was pro-gay. Nonetheless, she recognized her higher calling her Oath to defend the Colorado Constitution against all enemies, foreign and domestic. She took a stand that made her unpopular with her own party, her circle of friends, and even members of her own family.

4. The California Constitution, Article V Section 13, states: The Attorney General has the duty to see that the laws of the state are uniformly . . . enforced.

The American Heritage Dictionary defines the word uniform as:

1. Always the same, as in character or degree; unvarying.

2. Conforming to one principle, standard, or rule; consistent.

3. Being the same as or consonant with another or others.

4. Unvaried in texture, color, or design.

Proposition 215 was a political campaign. Its proponents have gone their several ways. It is a piece of history. The California Health & Safety Code 11362.5 is, however, the law, and you are by your Oath of Office and the California Constitution its primary proponent.

Please enforce California Health & Safety Code 11362.5 with the same vigor you do laws against murder, rape, and robbery. Please intercede and help defend me against the federal government with the considerable power of your office and of your persuasion.

I have studied the medical marijuana issue as journalist and as patient intensely for the past three years. If my input could be of any value, please do not hesitate to call.

Unfortunately, my current condition prevents me from volunteering to serve on your Medical Marijuana Commission. Might I nominate, however, someone with a significant depth of knowledge into both medical marijuana and politics. This person is Steve Kubby.

Mr. Kubby is a man whose doctor says is alive today because of medical marijuana. His knowledge of medical marijuana scientific, historical, and experiential is second to none.

As Libertarian candidate for Governor in the last election, Mr. Kubby knows California politics and media in California as few do. His ability to combine these attributes makes him the perfect member and tireless promoter of your Committee.

Yes, Mr. Kubby is facing state charges for medical marijuana cultivation, but that is no reason to keep him from your Committee. I understand Rev. Scott Imler is on you Committee. Mr. Imler openly grows (and buys and sells) more marijuana that Mr. Kubby is accused of. If there is room on your Committee for Rev. Imler, there is room for Mr. Kubby.

Allow me to close with Mr. Kubby’s letter, published in the March 3, 1999, issue of the Los Angeles Times:

Vasconcellos deserves high praise for his essay. This extraordinary statement is both courageous and historic, especially in light of his defense of McWilliams and other medical marijuana patients who are currently being persecuted by hostile federal officials.

Vasconcellos’ challenge to the federal government to respect the will of the people is the kind of genuine and inspired leadership that deserves our respect and support. It’s time to stop arresting sick people.

STEVE KUBBY Olympic Valley, Calif.

Aren’t these the words of a man you’d be proud to have on your Committee?

Sincerely,

Peter McWilliams
